Am I required to carry it?

Whether you must carry it depends on your exact address and loan — look your address up on FEMA's flood map. If the building is in a high-risk zone (any zone starting with A or V, such as A, AE, AH, AO or VE) and the loan comes from a federally regulated lender, or the purchase or construction gets federal financial assistance, federal law (42 U.S.C. §4012a) requires it. For context, 55.4% of Orange County's existing NFIP policies sit in those high-risk zones — not 55.4% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

How much does it cost here?

Among existing single-family primary-residence NFIP policies in Orange County, the median annual cost is $1,083, with the middle half between $854 and $1,265 (5,455 policies). This is what current policyholders pay — a new policy on a different building can differ. 45.8% of policyholders here pay a premium below FEMA's full “risk-based” premium: median full-risk premium $1,157 vs median premium charged $857 (premiums only, before fees); see below.

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half (p25–p75).

Coverage in force: $2,373,397,000 of building and $530,547,000 of contents coverage across all Orange County policies.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Two facts change your timing and your limits:

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so a policy bought today will not cover a flood this week. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

45.8% of 5,455 single-family policies pay a premium below FEMA's own full-risk premium; the median full-risk premium is $1,157 versus a median premium charged of $857. Both are premiums only; the costs above also include fees.

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$857
  • Median full-risk premium$1,157
  • Pay below full-risk45.8% of 5,455

Years to the full-risk price: By law most premiums cannot rise more than 18% a year (FloodSmart puts it at 18–25% for most policyholders); the cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. At the 18% cap, a policy at today's median premium ($857) would take at least about 2 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk premium ($1,157). This is the limit on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How much flood risk is here?

FEMA rates Orange County's coastal flood risk Relatively High and inland flood risk Very High — how this county compares with others, not odds for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskRelatively High
  • Inland flood riskVery High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. The rating multiplies expected flood loss by a community factor for social vulnerability and resilience; the percentile below is expected loss alone, so the two can differ. Coastal: expected annual flood loss above about 71% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $8,413,133 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Inland: expected annual flood loss above about 90% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $819,930,991 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Any loss figure is a whole-county estimate across all buildings, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Between 1978 and 2026, Orange County had 3,839 NFIP flood claims, which paid $21,147,012 in total.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 1997 ($3,194,090), 2010 ($3,162,145), 1995 ($2,613,484). Net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 3,839 claims since 1978 against 9,496 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Of 3,839 NFIP flood claims ever filed in Orange County, the average paid claim came to $10,381, and 46.9% were closed with no payment.

  • Average paid claim$10,381
  • Closed with no payment46.9%

FEMA lists reasons a claim closes without payment, such as damage below the deductible, no flood as the policy defines it, or seepage and drain backup the policy does not cover. The average is over claims that paid something; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Physical flood events recorded by the National Weather Service for this county (1996 on), separate from insured NFIP claims — it counts floods that happened, insured or not. Damage figures are NWS field estimates, not audited, and undercount in early years.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 9,496 policy units (from 8,819 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 8819/8819 fetched; claims: 3839/3839 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
